x: The Badami (Vatapi) Chalukyas ruled from about 543 CE, under Pulakeshin I, to 753 CE, when Dantidurga overthrew Kirtivarman II. The other ranges are reigns of single kings: Vikramaditya I, Pulakeshin II and Kirtivarman II.
t: Discriminate the dynasty's span from individual reigns.

x: Pulakeshin I performed the Ashvamedha, Kirtivarman I annexed the Kadambas, Gangas and Mauryas of Konkan, Mangalesha ruled between Kirtivarman I and Pulakeshin II, and Pulakeshin II took the title Dakshinapatheshwara, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the key achievement of each Badami Chalukya ruler.

x: Option C is incorrect: Kanchi was the Pallava capital. The Badami Chalukyas ruled from Vatapi, present-day Badami in Bagalkot district, Karnataka, and their power lay in the Deccan and South India.
t: Match each capital with its dynasty.

x: Both are true and R explains A: in the war with Harsha, usually dated 630–634 CE, Pulakeshin II checked Harshavardhana's southward advance on the Narmada.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the poet Ravikirti, author of the Aihole inscription, names Kalidasa and Bharavi because he claims to equal their fame.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: the Aihole inscription of 634 CE, on the Meguti Jain temple, was composed by the Jain poet Ravikirti in Sanskrit using the Southern Brahmi script, so the answer is I, II, III and IV.
t: Check each statement separately.
s:
Consider the following statements about the Aihole inscription:
I. It is dated 634 CE.
II. It is preserved at the Meguti Jain Temple.
III. It was composed by Ravikirti.
IV. It uses Sanskrit and Southern Brahmi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: The Lohnara inscription of 630 CE lists enemies defeated by Pulakeshin II but does not include Harsha. The Aihole inscription of 634 CE does record his victory over Harsha.
t: Discriminate the Lohnara inscription from the Aihole inscription.

x: Around 626 CE Pulakeshin II received an embassy from the Persian king Khusrau II, an exchange also linked to an Ajanta painting. The other years mark later reigns or events.
t: Recall the year of the Persian embassy.

x: Option B is incorrect: it was the Chalukya Vikramaditya I who restored Chalukya power. The Pallava Narasimhavarman I captured and destroyed Vatapi in 642 CE and took the title Vatapikonda.
t: Discriminate the Pallava conqueror from the Chalukya restorer.

x: Lohnara inscription (630 CE), Aihole inscription (634 CE), Narasimhavarman I's capture of Vatapi (642 CE), then Dantidurga's overthrow of Kirtivarman II (c. 753 CE), giving A, B, C, D.
t: Arrange the events by year.

x: A seventh-century inscription of Vikramaditya I dealing with land-grant practices was found at Madapura Lake in Davangere district, Karnataka. Aihole and the Meguti temple are known for the 634 CE record.
t: Recall the site of the recently found inscription.

x: Kirtivarman II (c. 746–753 CE) was the last Badami Chalukya ruler; the Rashtrakuta Dantidurga overthrew him. Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakuta line, and Vikramaditya II was Kirtivarman II's father.
t: Discriminate the last Chalukya king from the founder of the Rashtrakutas.

x: Both are true: the Badami Chalukyas often gave women high administrative posts, and Vijaya Bhattarika, queen of Chandraditya, governed the kingdom after his death.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Vijaya Bhattarika was Chandraditya's queen, Kumkumdevi was a Chalukya princess and sister of Vijayaditya who patronised a Jain basadi, Badami is known for rock-cut caves, and Pattadakal was a Chalukya temple centre, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the role of each person and site.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Vijaya Bhattarika
(b) Kumkumdevi
(c) Badami
(d) Pattadakal

List-II
(i) Chalukya princess, sister of Vijayaditya
(ii) Queen of Chandraditya
(iii) Rock-cut caves
(iv) Chalukya architectural centre

x: Both are true and R explains A: Badami has four rock-cut cave temples because Caves 1 to 3 are Hindu shrines and Cave 4 is Jain.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Ma-Twa-Lin (Matwalin) is the Chinese writer whose account describes China–India relations in the Chalukya period. Ravikirti and Bharavi were poets, and Khusrau II was a Persian king.
t: Eliminate the poets and the Persian king.

x: Badami (Vatapi) was the Chalukya capital, Kanchi the Pallava capital, Tanjore the Chola capital, and the Narmada the site where Pulakeshin II checked Harsha, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Match each place with its dynasty or event.

x: Pulakeshin I is the real founder of the Vatapi (Badami) Chalukya dynasty; he fortified Vatapi and performed the Ashvamedha. Kirtivarman I, Mangalesha and Pulakeshin II came after him.
t: Recall the founder of the dynasty.

x: Pulakeshin II took the title Dakshinapatheshwara, meaning Lord of the Deccan. Vatapikonda was the title of his Pallava enemy Narasimhavarman I.
t: Discriminate Pulakeshin II's title from his enemy's.

x: Option B is incorrect: the Aihole inscription is in Sanskrit, not Prakrit, written in Southern Brahmi. It was composed by Ravikirti and is the key source for Pulakeshin II.
t: Check the language of the inscription.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Vikramaditya II (c. 733–746 CE) defeated the Pallavas three times and took Kanchi, but his reign dates do not explain these victories.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Badami is known for rock-cut caves, Aihole for early experimental temples, Pattadakal (a UNESCO site) for Nagara and Dravida temples standing side by side, and Vesara is the name of the hybrid style, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the feature of each site and style.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Badami
(b) Aihole
(c) Pattadakal
(d) Vesara

List-II
(i) Name of the hybrid temple style
(ii) Rock-cut caves
(iii) Experimental or early temple architecture
(iv) UNESCO site with Nagara and Dravida temples side by side

x: Option A is correct: Vijaya Bhattarika, a poetess and queen of Chandraditya, issued two copper plates in her own name and ran the kingdom after his death. Option B describes Kumkumdevi.
t: Discriminate Vijaya Bhattarika from Kumkumdevi.

x: Pulakeshin I ruled c. 543–566 CE, Kirtivarman I c. 566–598 CE, Pulakeshin II 610–642 CE and Vikramaditya I c. 655–680 CE, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Arrange the rulers by reign.

x: All three are correct: Pulakeshin II is seen as the most capable and most powerful Chalukya ruler, and he and the Pallava Narasimhavarman I were great rivals, so the answer is I, II and III.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: The Aihole inscription is dated in the Saka era, year 556 (634 CE); it also gives a Kali era date. It does not use the Gupta, Vikrama or Harsha eras.
t: Recall the era used in the inscription.

x: The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi began as a branch of the Badami Chalukyas: Pulakeshin II placed his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana in charge of Vengi. The Kalyani Chalukyas were a later, separate branch.
t: Recall the parent line of the Vengi Chalukyas.

x: Option B is incorrect: the order is reversed. Vengi was the early Eastern Chalukya capital, and Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry) rose to importance later, under rulers like Rajaraja Narendra.
t: Check the order of the two capitals.

x: Option D is incorrect: Kubja Vishnuvardhana founded the Eastern Chalukya dynasty. Rajaraja Narendra was a later major ruler based at Rajamahendravaram and linked to the Chola royal family by marriage.
t: Discriminate the founder from the later ruler.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Nannaya, patronised by Rajaraja Narendra, began the Andhra Mahabharatam, the first major Telugu literary work, so the period is a landmark for Telugu literature.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Eastern Chalukyas were important in Andhra–Deccan politics and also had repeated dealings and wars with the Cholas, but their general importance does not by itself explain that conflict.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: Badami, seat of the parent Chalukya line, is in Karnataka, and Vengi, seat of the Eastern Chalukyas, is near Eluru in Andhra Pradesh.
t: Check the state of each capital.

x: A is true: Rajaraja Narendra ruled from Rajamahendravaram. B is false because it was his court poet Nannaya who began the Telugu Mahabharata; the king was the patron.
t: Discriminate the patron from the poet.

x: I and II are correct: the Eastern Chalukyas are the Chalukyas of Vengi, and Vengi in Andhra Pradesh was their core region. III is false because the Badami region of Karnataka belonged to the parent Badami Chalukyas.
t: Discriminate the Eastern Chalukya region from the parent line's region.

x: Kubja Vishnuvardhana founded the Eastern Chalukyas, Rajaraja Narendra was Nannaya's patron, Nannaya began the Telugu Mahabharata, and Matwalin wrote of China–India relations, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the role of each person.

x: Vengi was the Eastern Chalukya core region, Rajamahendravaram the later important centre, Badami the region of the parent Chalukya branch, and Andhra Pradesh the present state containing Vengi, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the role of each place.

x: The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi saw their succession tied up with the Cholas, the Cholas fought and intermarried with them, Kubja Vishnuvardhana founded the Eastern Chalukya line, and Kulottunga I was Rajendra Chalukya who united both lines, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Recall how the two dynasties merged.
s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
 a. Eastern Chalukyas
 b. Cholas
 c. Kubja Vishnuvardhana
 d. Kulottunga I

List-II
 i. Dynasty that repeatedly fought and intermarried with the Eastern Chalukyas

x: Three are correct: the Eastern Chalukyas branched from the Badami line, Kubja Vishnuvardhana was Pulakeshin II's brother, and Vengi was their core region. Statement 4 is false because Rajamahendravaram later became their important centre.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Rajendra Chalukya, who became the Chola emperor Kulottunga I in 1070 CE, was born of the Eastern Chalukya–Chola marriages and united the two royal lines.
t: Recall the ruler who joined the two lines.

x: Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakuta empire in 753 CE by overthrowing the Badami Chalukya Kirtivarman II. Krishna I, Govinda III and Amoghavarsha I were later rulers.

x: Dantidurga performed the Hiranyagarbha (golden womb) ritual at Ujjayini to raise his status. The Tripartite Struggle was a war, not a ritual.

t: Eliminate the Pratihara and Pala kings.

x: Option C is incorrect: Amoghavarsha I was born in 800 CE at Shribhavan, near the Narmada, in a military camp, not at Manyakheta. Manyakheta was the Rashtrakuta capital he built.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Kannauj was the symbol of imperial power in the north, and the Rashtrakutas' wish to control it drew them into the Tripartite Struggle with the Palas and Pratiharas.

s:
Assertion (A): The Rashtrakutas participated in the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj.
Reason (R): The Rashtrakutas, like the Palas and Pratiharas, sought control of Kannauj, the prestigious imperial city of north India.

x: Amoghavarsha I was born in 800 CE, at Shribhavan, in a military camp, and Manyakheta was the Rashtrakuta capital, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall each detail of Amoghavarsha I's birth.

x: The Jain scholar Jinasena wrote the Adipurana; he was a teacher at Amoghavarsha I's court. Amoghavarsha I himself wrote the Kavirajamarga.
t: Discriminate the author from his royal patron.

x: The Kailasa temple was a Rashtrakuta work, cut as Cave 16 at Ellora, built in the Dravidian style and built under Krishna I, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall each detail of the Kailasa temple.

x: The Kailasa (Kailasanatha) temple at Ellora was designed to look like Mount Kailasa, the home of Shiva. The other options are Rashtrakuta places, not the temple's model.
t: Recall what the temple's name refers to.

x: Three: Buddhist, Hindu and Jain rock-cut caves stand side by side at Ellora. Shakta is a Hindu sect the Rashtrakutas patronised, not a separate group of caves.
t: Recall the three cave groups at Ellora.

x: Both are true: the Kailasa temple was carved under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the 8th century, and it is Cave 16 at Ellora.
t: Recall the builder and the site of the Kailasa temple together.

Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Kailasa Temple was carved under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.

Consider the following statements:
I. Krishna I built the Kailasa Temple.

x: The Kailasa temple is a Shaiva rock-cut monument, Jinasena was the Jain author of the Adipurana, Dantidurga performed the Hiranyagarbha at Ujjayini, and Amoghavarsha I wrote the Kannada Kavirajamarga, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.

s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Kailasa Temple, Ellora
(b) Jinasena
(c) Hiranyagarbha ritual
(d) Kavirajamarga

(i) Shaiva rock-cut monument

x: Mahendravarman I (Pallava, c. 600–630 CE) came first, then Gopala (founder of the Pala dynasty, c. 750 CE), then Mihir Bhoja (Pratihara, c. 836–885 CE), giving B, C, A.
t: Arrange the rulers by period.

x: Govinda III defeated the Gurjara-Pratihara Nagabhata II on his northern campaign, during the Tripartite Struggle. Dantidurga and Krishna I came before him, and Amoghavarsha I was his son.
t: Recall which Rashtrakuta led the northern campaign.

x: The Chalukyas of Kalyani are called the Western Chalukyas, to set them apart from the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi. The Badami Chalukyas were the earlier parent line.
t: Discriminate the three Chalukya branches.

x: The Kalyani Chalukyas ruled from about 973 CE, when Tailapa II overthrew the Rashtrakutas, to 1195 CE. 543–753 CE is the Badami Chalukya period.
t: Recall the period of each Chalukya line.

x: A is true: the Kalyani Chalukyas built a distinctive Deccan cultural tradition. B is false because their tradition was rooted in the Deccan, not an exclusively north Indian one.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true and R explains A: mixing Dravida forms with Deccan innovations is exactly what produced the distinctive Kalyani Chalukya style.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: The Kasivisvesvara temple is at Lakkundi, the Mahadeva temple at Itagi and the Doddabasappa temple at Dambal, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Recall the site of each temple.

x: Option B is incorrect: Kalyani Chalukya temples have richly decorated doorways, not plain ones. Ornate pillars, intricate wall motifs and stepped superstructures are all correct features.
t: Check the feature in each statement.

x: Balanced proportions describe the architectural composition of Kalyani Chalukya temples. Language policy, literature and sculptural themes are not features of proportion.
t: Eliminate the options unrelated to architecture.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the subjects carved (deities, dancers, musicians, mythical figures) describe what was shown, not why the style became more ornate, dynamic and finely detailed.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: A is true: floral and geometric motifs appear in Kalyani Chalukya sculpture. B is false because the sculpture also showed dancers, musicians and mythical figures, not deities alone.

x: The Lakkundi–Gadag–Itagi group is a regional school of Kalyani Chalukya temple architecture and sculpture. It is not linked to succession, taxation or war.

x: Sanskrit and Kannada flourished under Kalyani Chalukya patronage: Bilhana and Vijnaneshwara wrote in Sanskrit, and Nagavarma II wrote in Kannada.

x: Someshvara III wrote the Manasollasa, Bilhana the Vikramankadeva Charita, Vijnaneshwara the Mitakshara and Nagavarma II the Kavyavalokana, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Kalyani Chalukya art is called a precursor of Hoysala art because it formed the direct link to the later Hoysala style.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Vijayalaya founded the Imperial Chola line in the mid-9th century by taking Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars. Aditya I, Parantaka I and Rajaraja I were later rulers.

 i. Rajaraja II

x: Both are true: Ayyavole 500 and Manigramam were merchant guilds of the Chola age, and Chola sea trade ran from Sri Lanka through the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra to Southeast Asia.

x: Rajaraja I (985), Rajendra I (1014), Kulottunga I (1070) and Rajendra III (1246), giving B, D, C, A.

x: Aditya I defeated the Pallava Aparajita, Parantaka I lost at Thakkolam to the Rashtrakutas, Rajendra I sent the naval expedition to Kadaram and Srivijaya, and Kulottunga I abolished tolls, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the key event of each ruler.

x: All four are correct: Chola temples follow the Dravida style, Chola bronzes such as Nataraja were cast by the lost-wax method, and the Cholas patronised both Tamil and Sanskrit literature, so the answer is I, II, III and IV.

x: Rajaraja I's Thanjavur inscription records his victory over the Chera fleet at Kandalur Salai, on the Kerala coast. That was his first major campaign.

x: Thakkolam was fought in 949 CE, Brihadeeswara completed in 1010 CE, the Kadaram–Srivijaya expedition sent in 1025 CE and Gangaikondacholapuram built around 1035 CE, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.

x: All four: Chola religious and artistic life centred on Shaivism and temple institutions, and temples supported music, dance and festivals.

x: I, II and IV are correct: Hoysala sculpture has detailed friezes and mythological scenes, and these are part of the distinctive Hoysala style. III is false because the sculpture is famous for its rich detail.

s:
Consider the following statements about Hoysala sculpture:
I. It includes highly detailed friezes.
II. It includes mythological depictions.
III. It is described as lacking decorative detail.
IV. It forms part of the distinctive Hoysala architectural style.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: Halebidu and Belur hold the main Hoysala monuments, and the Hoysala style blends Nagara and Dravida elements.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Both are true and R explains A: after Ballala III died fighting the Madurai Sultanate in 1343 CE, the Hoysala lands passed into the new Vijayanagara kingdom.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Hoysaleshwara is a Shiva temple, Chennakeshava a Vishnu temple, Halebidu is famous for Hoysala architecture, and Belur is where the Chennakeshava temple stands, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Match each temple with its deity and each place with its feature.

x: Option C is incorrect: the Yadavas (Seunas) were centred on Devagiri in the western Deccan. Warangal was the Kakatiya capital.

x: Warangal was the Kakatiya capital, Rudrama Devi the fourth independent Kakatiya ruler, Seuna another name for the Yadavas, and Devagiri the Yadava centre, giving a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.

List-I
(a) Kakatiya capital
(b) Rudrama Devi

(ii) Alternative name of Yadavas

x: All three are correct: Rudrama Devi was the fourth independent Kakatiya ruler and she fought off the Pandyas and the Eastern Gangas, so the answer is I, II and III.

x: A is true: the Yadavas ruled from about 1187 to 1317 CE. B is false because they ruled the western Deccan from Devagiri, not eastern India.

x: The Kakatiyas ruled the eastern Deccan from Warangal in the 12th–14th centuries. The Seunas (Yadavas) ruled the western Deccan, and the Eastern Gangas ruled Odisha.

x: Option C is incorrect: Devagiri was the Yadava capital. The Kakatiyas ruled the eastern Deccan from Warangal in the 12th–14th centuries.

x: Option D is incorrect: Rudrama Devi was herself a Kakatiya ruler of Warangal, so she could not defeat the Kakatiyas. She defeated the Eastern Gangas of Odisha, the Pandyas and the Seunas of Devagiri.

Consider the following statements:
I. Rudradeva is also referred to as Pratap Rudradeva I.
II. Mahadeva came after Rudradeva.
III. Ganapati Dev was the father of Rudrama Devi.
IV. Rudrama Devi was the 4th independent Kakatiya ruler.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: The Kakatiyas ruled the eastern Deccan, their capital was Warangal, the Seunas ruled from Devagiri, and the Eastern Gangas ruled Orissa, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Match each dynasty with its region or capital.

x: Rudradeva was also called Prataparudra I, Mahadeva came after him, Ganapati Deva was Rudrama Devi's father, and Rudrama Devi was Ganapati Deva's daughter, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the order of Kakatiya rulers.

x: Three are correct: Rudrama Devi was Ganapati Deva's daughter, the fourth independent Kakatiya ruler and a woman ruler. IV is false because Prataparudra I is another name of Rudradeva.
t: Discriminate Rudrama Devi from Rudradeva.

t: Discriminate a dynasty from its rulers and capital.
